lesson.title: Mass Extinctions: When the Tree of Life Loses Its Branches
lesson.summary: A mass extinction is a relatively short interval in Earth's history during which a large fraction of species disappear worldwide, dramatically reshaping the macroevolutionary trajectory of life.
lesson.body:
Extinction is happening constantly at a low, ongoing rate, sometimes called the background extinction rate, as individual species fail to adapt to local changes or get outcompeted. A mass extinction is different in scale and speed: a geologically brief period in which a large percentage of species across many unrelated groups and environments disappear at roughly the same time. Paleontologists identify these events in the fossil record as fossil evidence showing many lineages vanishing abruptly at the same rock layer, rather than the slow, steady turnover expected from background extinction alone.

The most severe mass extinction identified in the fossil record occurred at the end of the Permian period, about 252 million years ago, sometimes called the Great Dying. Estimates vary somewhat between studies, but commonly cited figures suggest that roughly 90 percent or more of marine species were lost, along with a large fraction of terrestrial vertebrate species as well. The leading hypothesis points to massive volcanic activity in what is now Siberia (the Siberian Traps), which released enormous quantities of carbon dioxide and other gases over a relatively short geological interval, contributing to rapid warming, ocean acidification, and oxygen depletion in the oceans. Researchers continue to debate the precise combination of causes and their relative timing, so this should be understood as the best supported current explanation rather than a fully settled certainty.

A more recent and better documented example is the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction, about 66 million years ago, which ended the reign of the non-avian dinosaurs along with many other groups, including the ammonites. This event is strongly supported by physical evidence: a thin layer of clay found worldwide that is unusually enriched in iridium, an element rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids, along with the identification of a large impact crater at Chicxulub on Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula dated to the same time. The impact is thought to have thrown enormous amounts of debris into the atmosphere, blocking sunlight and disrupting food chains on a global scale.

Mass extinctions matter for macroevolution because they do more than simply remove species. By eliminating dominant groups, they open up ecological opportunities for the lineages that survive, often triggering new rounds of adaptive radiation. The extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs, for instance, is closely tied to the subsequent diversification of mammals into ecological roles that had previously been occupied by dinosaurs. In this way, mass extinctions act as resets that punctuate the longer term, more gradual patterns of macroevolutionary change.

Paleontologists traditionally recognize five major mass extinctions over roughly the last 540 million years, often called the Big Five, of which the Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous-Paleogene events are two of the best studied. Some scientists have raised the question of whether current, human driven biodiversity loss could represent the beginning of a sixth mass extinction, but this remains a matter of ongoing scientific discussion rather than a fully resolved conclusion, and it is mentioned here only to note that the concept of mass extinction is not purely a topic of the deep past.
